blurb: Chemistry, physics and biology jokes, tested in the lab for maximum groan

questions.q: Why can't you trust an atom?
questions.fact: Bonus: What did the scientist say when she found two helium atoms? HeHe.
questions.src: classic (reserved for Lab Rats); premise: atoms make up all ordinary matter; He is the symbol for helium

questions.q: Why are chemists so good at solving problems?
questions.fact: Bonus: I'd tell you a chemistry joke, but I know I wouldn't get a reaction.
questions.src: classic; premise: a solution is a substance dissolved in a liquid

questions.q: Why do scientists always look for things twice?
questions.fact: Bonus: Why does the microscope always overreact? It blows everything out of proportion.
questions.src: classic (replaces the No-bell Prize door knocker, which repeats J1 Knock Knock's 'Nobel who? No bell' question and its 'no-bell prize' bonus); premise: research = re-search, to search again; microscopes magnify

questions.q: What does a subatomic duck say?
questions.fact: Bonus: What did the nuclear physicist have for lunch? Fission chips.
questions.src: classic (replaces the thermometer 'more degrees' joke, which repeated J3 Space Cadets' sun 'millions of degrees' pun); premise: quarks are subatomic particles that make up protons and neutrons; fission is splitting atoms

questions.q: I'm reading a book about anti-gravity. ___
questions.fact: Bonus: Why did the arm bone love jokes? It found everything humerus.
questions.src: classic; premise: the humerus is the upper arm bone

questions.q: What do biologists wear to look sharp?
questions.fact: Bonus: Why do chemists like working with ammonia? It's pretty basic stuff.
questions.src: classic; premise: genes are units of heredity; ammonia is a base

questions.q: A neutron walks into a cafe and asks how much a coffee costs. The barista says ___
questions.fact: Bonus: A photon checks into a hotel. Any bags? 'No thanks, I'm traveling light.'
questions.src: classic; premise: neutrons have no electric charge; photons are particles of light

questions.q: What do you call a tooth in a glass of water?
questions.fact: The pun: a molar is a back tooth, and in chemistry a one-molar solution has one mole of a substance per liter.
questions.src: classic; premise: a molar is a back tooth; a 1 molar (1 M) solution has 1 mole of solute per liter of solution

questions.q: Two atoms bump into each other. One says, 'I lost an electron!' The other asks, 'Are you sure?' ___
questions.fact: Bonus: Want to hear a joke about sodium? Na.
questions.src: classic; premise: an atom that loses an electron becomes a positive ion; Na is the symbol for sodium

questions.q: What did the cell say right after it split in two?
options: Now there are two of us
questions.fact: Bonus: Oxygen and potassium did a group project together. It went OK.
questions.src: original; premise: cells reproduce by dividing in two; O is oxygen, K is potassium

questions.q: Biology is the only science where ___
questions.fact: Bonus: Why did the virus get a million followers? Everything it posted went viral.
questions.src: classic; premise: cells multiply by dividing

questions.q: A quantum physicist gets pulled over. 'Do you know how fast you were going?' He says ___
options: No, but I know where I am
questions.fact: The pun: in quantum physics you can't know a particle's exact speed and exact spot at once. It's called the uncertainty principle.
questions.src: classic (folk physics joke, adapted without naming Heisenberg); premise: Heisenberg uncertainty principle, position and momentum

blurb: Jokes from every field, court, course and lane. No refs required.

questions.q: Why did the golfer bring two pairs of pants?
options: In case it rained all day
To look good in the photos
In case he got a hole in one
To match his new golf bag
questions.fact: Bonus: What's a golfer's favorite letter? Tee.
questions.src: classic; premise: a hole in one is sinking the ball with the first shot; golf balls sit on tees

questions.q: Where do baseball catchers sit at dinner?
options: At the end of the table
questions.fact: Bonus: What did the baseball glove say to the ball? Catch you later.
questions.src: classic; premise: the catcher crouches behind home plate

questions.q: Why did the softball player bring string to the game?
options: So she could tie the score
questions.fact: Bonus: Which sport is always getting into trouble? Bad-minton.
questions.src: classic

questions.q: What has 18 legs and catches flies?
questions.fact: Bonus: Why is tennis such a noisy sport? Every player raises a racket.
questions.src: classic; premise: a baseball team fields nine players (18 legs) who catch fly balls; hockey fields 6 (12 legs), soccer 11 (22 legs)

questions.q: Why do basketball players love cookies?
questions.fact: Bonus: Why are basketball players such messy eaters? They're always dribbling.
questions.src: classic

questions.q: I don't play soccer because I'm good at it. I just do it for ___
questions.fact: Bonus: What lights up a soccer stadium? A soccer match.
questions.src: classic, adapted

questions.q: What do runners eat before a big race?
questions.fact: Bonus: Why did the football coach go to the bank? To get his quarter back.
questions.src: classic

questions.q: I gave up archery. There were just too many ___
questions.fact: The pun: to shoot, an archer draws back the bowstring. A drawback is also a downside.
questions.src: classic one-liner; premise: archers draw back the bowstring before releasing

questions.q: Why was the stadium so hot after the game?
questions.fact: Bonus: Why can't track stars listen to vinyl? They keep breaking records.
questions.src: classic

questions.q: My ski lessons started out great, but then ___
questions.fact: Bonus: Why is Cinderella so bad at soccer? She keeps running away from the ball.
questions.src: classic one-liner, adapted; Cinderella is a folk tale

questions.q: I almost quit the hurdles team, but then ___
questions.fact: Bonus: I'd tell you a yoga joke, but it's a bit of a stretch.
questions.src: classic one-liner, adapted

questions.q: I shot 160 in golf and bowled a 90 this week. If only I could ___
questions.fact: Bonus: Why do basketball players never go on vacation? They'd get called for traveling.
questions.src: original; premise: in golf the lower score is better, in bowling the higher score is better (300 max); traveling is a basketball violation

blurb: Computer, phone and internet jokes, with no hold music

questions.q: Why did the computer go to the doctor?
questions.fact: Bonus: Why was the computer cold? It left its Windows open.
questions.src: classic

questions.q: Why was the computer so tired when it got home?
questions.fact: Bonus: Why was the computer so smart? It listened to its motherboard.
questions.src: classic

questions.q: What does a baby computer call its father?
questions.fact: Bonus: What did the computer do at lunchtime? It had a byte.
questions.src: classic; 'Data' sounds like 'Dada'

questions.q: Why did the web browser go broke?
questions.fact: The pun: a browser's cache saves bits of websites so pages load faster, and 'cache' sounds just like 'cash.'
questions.src: original twist on a classic programmer pun; premise: browsers keep a cache of site files

questions.q: What's a computer's favorite snack?
questions.fact: Bonus: Why did the computer go to the beach? To surf the web.
questions.src: classic

questions.q: Why did the phone wear glasses?
questions.fact: Bonus: Why did the email feel so clingy? It had too many attachments.
questions.src: classic

questions.q: What do you get when you cross a computer with a lifeguard?
questions.fact: Bonus: How do trees get online? They log in.
questions.src: classic

questions.q: What's a computer's favorite kind of beat?
questions.fact: Bonus: Why is the keyboard always so tired? It works two shifts.
questions.src: classic; premise: an algorithm is a set of steps a computer follows; keyboards have two Shift keys

questions.q: I set my password to 'incorrect.' Now when I forget it, the computer tells me ___
options: to try again in a minute
questions.fact: Bonus: What's a computer's least favorite food? Spam.
questions.src: classic (anonymous internet joke)

questions.q: Our Wi-Fi was down for an hour, so I had to talk to my family. They ___
questions.fact: Bonus: Why did the robot go on vacation? To recharge its batteries.
questions.src: classic (anonymous internet joke), adapted

questions.q: Why do programmers prefer dark mode?
questions.fact: Bonus: A USB plug has only two sides, yet it always takes me three tries to plug it in.
questions.src: classic programmer joke; premise: software errors are called bugs, and light draws insects

questions.q: I told my phone's voice assistant, 'Call me a taxi.' It said ___
options: OK. From now on, you're Taxi
Your ride is on the way
questions.fact: Bonus: Why did the computer squeak? Someone stepped on its mouse.
questions.src: classic 'call me a cab' joke, updated for voice assistants

blurb: Friendly jokes from the Stone Age to the Statue of Liberty

questions.q: Where was the Declaration of Independence signed?
questions.fact: Bonus: Why was the printing press such a hit? It made a great impression.
questions.src: classic; premise: signed in Philadelphia, signatures below the text; printing presses press ink onto paper

questions.q: Why were the early Middle Ages called the Dark Ages?
questions.fact: Bonus: What was the most popular dance in 1776? The Indepen-dance.
questions.src: classic; premise: 'Dark Ages' is an old (now debated) name for the early Middle Ages, and the joke only says it was called that

questions.q: Which old English king invented the fireplace?
questions.fact: The pun: Alfred the Great ruled Wessex in the 800s, and a grate is the iron rack that holds logs in a fireplace.
questions.src: classic; premise: Alfred the Great, king of Wessex 871-899; Edward the Elder (899-924), Ethelred the Unready (978-1016) and William the Conqueror (1066-1087) were real English kings

questions.q: How was the Roman Empire cut in half?
options: With a line on a map
questions.fact: Bonus: Why did the medieval king go to the dentist? To get his teeth crowned.
questions.src: classic; premise: the Roman Empire was split into Eastern and Western halves (395 AD); Caesar became an imperial title

questions.q: How did the Vikings send secret messages?
questions.fact: Bonus: Why did the pyramid builders finally stop? They got to the point.
questions.src: classic; premise: Vikings were Norse; pyramids rise to a point

questions.q: What came after the Stone Age and the Bronze Age?
questions.fact: Bonus: Why did the cave painters pick such big caves? They wanted to draw a crowd.
questions.src: classic; premise: Stone, Bronze, Iron Age sequence; prehistoric cave paintings are real

questions.q: Why do visitors love the Liberty Bell?
options: It's all it's cracked up to be
It sits in a big glass hall
questions.fact: The pun: the Liberty Bell in Philadelphia has a famous crack, and being 'all it's cracked up to be' means living up to the hype.
questions.src: original; premise: the Liberty Bell is cracked and on public display in the glass-walled Liberty Bell Center, Philadelphia; cast 1752-53, before 1776

questions.q: Why is the Leaning Tower of Pisa so agreeable?
options: It has seen it all before
questions.fact: Bonus: What's the hardest part of visiting the Great Wall of China? Getting around it.
questions.src: original; premise: the tower began tilting during construction in the 1100s; the Great Wall is thousands of miles long

questions.q: What's the first thing Queen Elizabeth I did after she took the throne?
questions.fact: Bonus: I wanted to be a history teacher, but there was no future in it.
questions.src: classic; premise: Elizabeth I became queen in 1558

questions.q: What happened at the Boston Tea Party?
questions.fact: Bonus: What kind of tea did the American colonists want? Liber-tea.
questions.src: classic; premise: in 1773 colonists dumped British tea into Boston Harbor

questions.q: I studied for years to become an archaeologist, but now my career ___
questions.fact: Bonus: My friend says history class is boring. I told him that's old news.
questions.src: classic one-liner, told in first person; premise: archaeologists dig up ruins

questions.q: I'd tell you a long joke about ancient Mesopotamia, but I'd just ___
questions.fact: The pun: Babylon was a great city of ancient Mesopotamia, and 'Babylon' sounds just like 'babble on.'
questions.src: classic; premise: Babylon was in Mesopotamia (modern Iraq)

blurb: Math and number jokes that always add up, eventually

questions.q: Why was six afraid of seven?
questions.fact: Bonus: What do you call a man who spends all summer at the beach? A tangent.
questions.src: classic; premise: a tangent is a line that touches a curve

questions.q: What did the zero say to the eight?
questions.fact: Bonus: What do you call friends who love math? Algebros.
questions.src: classic

questions.q: Why is the obtuse angle always so upset?
questions.fact: Bonus: Why can't you trust someone holding graph paper? They're plotting something.
questions.src: classic; premise: an obtuse angle is more than 90 degrees, so never a right angle

questions.q: Why don't people ever talk about the number 288?
questions.fact: The pun: a gross is an old word for 144, a dozen dozens. So 288 is two gross.
questions.src: classic; premise: a gross = 144, 2 x 144 = 288; 288 is not prime

questions.q: What did the calculator say to the student?
questions.fact: Bonus: Why was the math book sad? It had too many problems.
questions.src: classic

questions.q: What's a math teacher's favorite place in New York City?
questions.fact: Bonus: Why did the student do multiplication on the floor? The teacher said not to use tables.
questions.src: classic; premise: Times Square is in New York City

questions.q: What do you call an empty parrot cage?
questions.fact: Bonus: Who invented fractions? Henry the 1/8th.
questions.src: classic (replaces Sir Cumference, the title character of a well-known children's math book series); premise: a polygon is a closed shape with straight sides, and 'Polly' is the stock parrot name, so 'Polly gone'; Henry VIII

questions.q: Why did the number get upset when someone called it average?
options: It thought it was the median
It was way out of its range
It knew it was above average
That was a mean thing to say
questions.fact: Bonus: What do you call a number that can't sit still? A roamin' numeral.
questions.src: classic, adapted; premise: the mean is the average; median, mode and range are other statistics

questions.q: Parallel lines have so much in common. It's a shame they'll ___
questions.fact: Bonus: Why wasn't the number 4 invited to the party? It was too square.
questions.src: classic; premise: parallel lines never meet; 4 is a square number

questions.q: Studies show that five out of four people ___
questions.fact: Bonus: There's a fine line between a numerator and a denominator.
questions.src: classic one-liner; premise: the line in a fraction separates numerator and denominator

questions.q: Why is pi a terrible seatmate on a long flight?
options: It goes on and on forever
questions.fact: Bonus: Why does everyone like the circle? It's so well-rounded.
questions.src: original twist on a classic; premise: pi is irrational and its digits never end; 'well-rounded' means having many good qualities

questions.q: How do you make seven even?
questions.fact: Bonus: There are 10 kinds of people: those who understand binary and those who don't.
questions.src: classic; premise: 'seven' minus the s spells 'even'; 10 in binary is 2

blurb: Music and instrument jokes, from the garage band to the grand piano

questions.q: Why did the singer climb a ladder?
questions.fact: Bonus: Why did the music note go to school? To get a little sharper.
questions.src: classic; premise: a sharp raises a note a half step

questions.q: What has lots of keys but can't open a single door?
questions.fact: Bonus: What did the guitar say to the guitarist? Stop picking on me.
questions.src: classic riddle; premise: a standard piano has 88 keys

questions.q: Why did the drummer take a long nap after the show?
questions.fact: Bonus: Why are pianos so classy? They're either upright or grand.
questions.src: classic; premise: pianos come as uprights and grands

questions.q: What do you call a musician with lots of problems?
questions.fact: The pun: the treble clef marks the high notes in music, and 'trebled' sounds a lot like 'troubled.'
questions.src: classic; premise: the treble clef is used for higher notes

questions.q: What do you get when you cross a fridge with a radio?
questions.fact: Bonus: Why did the singer make a great baseball player? She had perfect pitch.
questions.src: classic

questions.q: What's a balloon's least favorite kind of music?
questions.fact: Bonus: What did the drummer name his twin daughters? Anna One and Anna Two.
questions.src: classic

questions.q: Why was the violin so nervous before the concert?
questions.fact: Bonus: Why are music notes never lonely? They always have the staff around.
questions.src: classic; premise: violin strings are tightened to pitch; notes are written on a staff

questions.q: How do you fix a broken tuba?
questions.fact: Bonus: What kind of music do shoes like best? Sole music.
questions.src: classic; 'a tuba glue' sounds like 'a tube of glue'

questions.q: I used to play the piano by ear. Now ___
questions.fact: Bonus: Why did the composer spend all day in bed? He was writing sheet music.
questions.src: classic one-liner (anonymous; Barry Popik traces versions with no known author)

questions.q: How do you make a bandstand?
questions.fact: Bonus: Why was the trumpet so annoying at parties? It kept tooting its own horn.
questions.src: classic

questions.q: My band is called Duvet. We're mostly a ___
questions.fact: Bonus: I wrote a song about my guitar. I hope it strikes a chord.
questions.src: classic one-liner, adapted; premise: a cover band plays other artists' songs; a duvet goes in a cover

questions.q: There's a new band called 1023 Megabytes. Sadly, ___
options: they haven't had a gig yet
questions.fact: The pun: in the binary count computers use, 1,024 megabytes make a gigabyte, so 1,023 is one short of a gig.
questions.src: classic internet joke; premise: 1 GB = 1,024 MB in the binary convention (1 GiB = 1,024 MiB); disk makers often use 1,000
